system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-02-27 20:15:00 to 2175-02-28 17:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy following a recent ERCP for common bile duct stone removal. The surgery was performed successfully on 2174-09-29. Postoperatively, he experienced right shoulder pain, prompting an orthopedic consultation and joint aspiration, which ruled out recurrent septic arthritis. He also developed transient urinary retention requiring catheterization and was started on tamsulosin, after which he successfully voided with a low post-void residual. His pain was managed with a multimodal regimen, and his liver function tests improved during the stay. He was discharged home on 2174-10-02 in good condition with updated medications and follow-up instructions.
problems: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis, without mention of obstruction
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ male with known esophageal varices, presenting with
upper GI bleed.

COMPARISON:  CTA abdomen and pelvis ___.

FINDINGS:  The liver is nodular in contour, compatible with cirrhosis.  Within
the right lobe of the liver, possibly segment V, there is an 8-mm rounded
echogenic lesion, without demonstrable color flow.  This is incompletely
characterized.  No additional lesions are identified.  The main, left, and
right portal veins demonstrate directionally appropriate flow.  The main
hepatic artery demonstrates sharp systolic upstrokes and normal diastolic
flow. The hepatic veins are patent.  Patient is status post cholecystectomy. 
There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilatation with the CBD
measuring 2 mm.  A trace amount of perihepatic free fluid is noted.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Cirrhotic liver, with an indeterminate 8-mm echogenic lesion within the
right lobe of the liver, possibly segment V.  This lesion should be further
evaluated with an MRI as hepatocellular carcinoma is not excluded.

2.  Patent portal venous system.

3.  Trace perihepatic free fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, your hospitalist. I understand you came in because of some blood in your vomit last week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a little streak of blood. I was worried, especially with my liver condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. Given your history of Hep C and esophageal varices, even a small amount of blood can be concerning. We’ve started you on an IV medication called pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid and lower the risk of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My hematocrit was down a lot—from 43 to 32. Is that from bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned it might be due to a slow bleed, possibly from your varices. But your vital signs are stable, and your repeat labs show your hematocrit hasn’t dropped further—31.6, then 30.9. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any more blood since then. No black stools either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We checked your stool here and it was negative for blood. We’ll keep monitoring your blood counts. Your liver ultrasound showed your cirrhosis is still present, and we saw a small 8mm spot in the liver that we’ll need to follow up on with an MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An MRI? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a precaution. The spot could be harmless, but with cirrhosis, we want to rule out early liver cancer. Your liver clinic will help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up. I also haven’t been taking my water pills—furosemide and spironolactone—for about a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That explains the 25-pound weight gain, increased belly size, and leg swelling. We gave you a dose of IV lasix tonight, and you’ve already had good urine output. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped them before a long drive. I didn’t want to stop too often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but skipping them can lead to fluid buildup, which increases pressure in your liver and could worsen bleeding risk. We’ll restart both diuretics tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your latest hematocrit is up to 34.9—improving. Your reticulocyte count is also up, which means your body is making new red blood cells. That suggests the bleeding has stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. So I’m not going to need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at this time. You’re stable, and your counts are trending up. We think the improvement may also be from losing excess fluid—your blood isn’t as diluted now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to discharge you today. We’ve adjusted some medications—like lowering your fluoxetine and changing how you take spironolactone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as long as you take your medications, especially the diuretics daily and check your weight. If you feel dizzy, see blood in your stool, or your weight spikes, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MRI for the liver spot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver clinic will schedule it. It’s just a precaution. Also, keep taking your lactulose and rifaximin for your liver, and the omeprazole to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for evaluation of an upper gastrointestinal bleed after reporting blood-tinged emesis and a drop in hematocrit from 43.5 to 32.7. Given his history of Hep C cirrhosis and esophageal varices, he was monitored closely with serial hematocrits, which stabilized and improved to 34.9, suggesting no ongoing active bleeding. He was continued on IV pantoprazole and observed without need for transfusion. He had significant fluid retention due to noncompliance with diuretics, having gained 25 pounds recently; after receiving IV furosemide and restarting spironolactone, he had good urine output and symptom improvement. An abdominal ultrasound revealed cirrhosis and an 8-mm indeterminate liver lesion, prompting a recommendation for MRI follow-up. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout and was discharged home with medication adjustments and instructions to resume all prescribed therapies, including diuretics, and to follow up in the liver clinic.
